summary: The macro-architecture is genuinely solid and improving: process boundaries are clean (contextIsolation/sandbox on, renderer never touches electron/ipcRenderer directly, single preload), IPC is contract-disciplined end-to-end (shared contracts.ts → BridgeResult<T> discriminated union → preload casts → window.appBridge typed via the same contracts), handlers are split into 5 cohesive domain modules with DI'd session/permission guards, and a madge scan of 354 files finds exactly one circular dependency — a benign type-only cycle. Strangler decomposition is visibly working: the performance domain is fanned out into ~10 focused services and renderer screens are being pulled apart into subdirectories (site-management 39, allowance-management 24 modules). However, the architecture's load-bearing data-integrity seams remain broken in exactly the places a payroll app cannot afford: JSON restore still re-creates only a hardcoded 28-table list while backup dumps ALL tables, silently dropping allowance_approvals / allowance_proposal_approvals / hidden_approved_performance_rows / access_logs; rate-version selection still calls the date-ignorant selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion before the date-aware one; duty interpretation is still forked (time-window classification in restore vs literal-letter match in the parser) over an unconstrained dutyCode: string the type system cannot police; and there are still zero SQL foreign keys to backstop any of it. Several god-files persist (PerformanceManagementScreen 123KB, allowance-document-export 113KB, database-migration 103KB). The new CI workflow (added today) is a real structural improvement but is not yet wired into the publish path. Net: the architecture supports safe incremental change at the module/IPC boundary, but the single-source-of-truth and data-restore seams are unsafe and unchanged from the prior audit.
strengths: Clean main/preload/renderer/shared boundaries: main.ts:184-189 sets contextIsolation:true, nodeIntegration:false, sandbox:true; Grep confirms renderer screens never import electron/ipcRenderer (0 occurrences in the 123KB PerformanceManagementScreen).

Disciplined IPC contract: src/shared/bridge/contracts.ts defines typed Bridge interfaces + BridgeResult<T> discriminated union; preload/index.ts casts every ipcRenderer.invoke to the contract return type; renderer/vite-env.d.ts:14-16 declares window.appBridge with the same shared types — the type contract is closed end-to-end.

IPC handlers are decomposed into 5 cohesive domain modules (register-core/workforce/operations/performance/allowance ~111 channels) wired in main.ts:248-281 via dependency-injected guards (withSession, withActionPermission, withAdmin) and shared ipc-handler-helpers.ts runIpcAction wrappers.

Strong Strangler-vs-rewrite posture: register-performance-handlers.ts:7-27 pulls from ~10 small focused services (performance-approval-flow, performance-queue, performance-approved-row-management, performance-startup-recovery, etc.) rather than one monolith; renderer screens decomposing into subdirectories (site-management 39, allowance-management 24, dashboard 17, operations-management 13 modules).

Excellent dependency hygiene: madge over 354 ts/tsx files finds exactly ONE circular dependency, and it is a type-only cycle (model.ts:4 `import type` document-template.ts ↔ document-template.ts:5 `import type` model.ts) — erased at compile, zero runtime risk.
Domain money logic is correctly isolated in src/shared/domain (calculation.ts, allowance-service.ts, rounding.ts) and reused by both renderer selectors and main services rather than duplicated.
weaknesses: Data-restore seam is asymmetric and lossy: database-backup-service.ts:49 dumps ALL user tables via sqlite_master, but importJsonBackupIntoCurrentDatabase iterates only the hardcoded JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER (database-migration-service.ts:74-104), so 4 pay/approval/audit tables are silently dropped on restore.

No single-source-of-truth for duty interpretation: dutyCode is an unconstrained `string` (model.ts:119,242); restore classifies duty by TIME WINDOW ignoring the literal letter (monthly-schedule-restore-service.ts:281-318), while the parser matches the literal dutyCode string (schedule-return-performance-parser.ts:701-714) — two divergent truths the type system cannot reconcile.

Rate-version selection composes date-ignorant logic ahead of date-aware logic: approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:115 calls selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions) (allowance-rate-service.ts:33-44, sorts by updatedAt, ignores workDate) BEFORE the workDate-aware selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion fallback — backdated pay can use the wrong rate.

Persistent god-files raise change risk: PerformanceManagementScreen.tsx (123KB / 3 sibling modules only), allowance-document-export-service.ts (113KB), database-migration-service.ts (103KB), operations-storage-service.ts (76KB), schedule-return-performance-parser.ts (56KB).

Dead architectural logic left in a load-bearing parser: resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable (schedule-return-performance-parser.ts:725-766) is still called at :1274 but its loop body only `continue`s and it unconditionally returns scheduleItem:null — a no-op masquerading as a holiday resolver.

No referential integrity at the storage layer: zero FOREIGN KEY declarations anywhere in src/ — table relationships are enforced only by hand-written service code, so an incomplete restore or orphaned row cannot be caught by the DB.

Quality gate still not on the production path: the new .github/workflows/ci.yml runs typecheck+test on push/PR, but release:publish (package.json:54) runs only build + release:check (file/env/manifest validation) — no test run — and git shows zero recent merge commits, so there is no enforced PR review before a release.

criticalFindings.title: JSON restore re-creates only a hardcoded table list, silently dropping 4 pay/approval/audit tables
criticalFindings.detail: Backup dumps every user table (database-backup-service.ts:45-55 via sqlite_master), but importJsonBackupIntoCurrentDatabase iterates only JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER (database-migration-service.ts:2787-2794), a fixed 28-name list (74-104) that omits allowance_approvals, allowance_proposal_approvals, hidden_approved_performance_rows, and access_logs. A restore therefore silently discards approval/pay history and the audit log. This is the single most dangerous architectural defect for a payroll app and is unchanged since the prior audit.

verification.finding: JSON restore re-creates only a hardcoded 28-table list, silently dropping 4 pay/approval/audit tables (allowance_approvals, allowance_proposal_approvals, hidden_approved_performance_rows, access_logs)
verification.reasoning:
Traced the full backup-and-restore path in 0.4.30 source and confirmed the defect is real, still present, and if anything slightly UNDER-stated.

BACKUP SIDE (asymmetry source): database-backup-service.ts listUserTableNames() (38-56) selects EVERY non-sqlite_% table from sqlite_master with no exclusion list. buildJsonBackupSnapshot (84-101) keys each by its exact table name (accumulator[table.name] = table.rows). So all 4 tables ARE dumped into the JSON backup. Confirmed via grep: the backup file contains no JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER / exclude / skip logic.

RESTORE SIDE (the drop): importJsonBackupIntoCurrentDatabase (database-migration-service.ts:2773-2844) iterates ONLY JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER (loop at 2787-2794), a fixed 28-name const (74-104). I grepped the ENTIRE migration service file for the 4 table names: zero matches. They are neither in the list nor handled by any other code path in restore.

THE 4 TABLES ARE REAL PERSISTENT TABLES HOLDING IRREPLACEABLE DATA (sqlite-storage-service.ts): allowance_approvals (585-599) = per-row pay approval decisions w/ processor + comment; allowance_proposal_approvals (607-624) = monthly 품의 approvals incl. total_allowance_amount + snapshot; hidden_approved_performance_rows (502-511) = approval-state for hidden approved rows; access_logs (349-361) = the audit log. All payroll/approval/audit history.

SEVERITY IS ACTUALLY UNDER-STATED, NOT OVER-STATED: I verified the restore mechanism is NOT an insert-into-existing-live-DB (which would leave old rows intact). runDatabaseMigrationUpdate (3063-3134) creates a FRESH empty temp DB (restore-{ts}.sqlite, 3085-3088), imports only the 28 tables into it (the 4 stay empty), then calls replaceDatabaseFileAtomically(currentSettings.databasePath, tempDatabasePath) at 3108 — a full file SWAP that destroys the live DB and replaces it with one where the 4 tables are empty. So restore = outright loss of pay-approval and audit history, with no in-app indication. The only mitigation is an auto pre-restore backup taken at 3084 (runDatabaseBackupNow), but that just means the lost data sits orphaned in a separate JSON backup that the restore code itself will never reimport.

NOT FIXED IN 0.4.30: git -S on JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER shows last touch 2026-03-24 (1b711e2); no later commit altered the import list. Cited line numbers match exactly (74-104 list, 2787-2794 loop, backup 45-55/38-56). PRIOR STATUS still-open is correct -> STILL-OPEN.

criticalFindings.title: Rate-version selection ignores workDate (backdated pay can use the wrong multiplier)
criticalFindings.detail: toRateTable composes selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions) FIRST (approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:115), which sorts active versions by updatedAt/createdAt and ignores workDate entirely (allowance-rate-service.ts:33-44). The workDate-aware selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion is only a fallback (:116-119). So when a newer rate version exists, retroactive/backdated work dates are priced with the latest rate instead of the one effective on workDate.

verification.finding: Rate-version selection ignores workDate (backdated pay can use the wrong multiplier)
verification.reasoning:
The cited lines are literally accurate: toRateTable (approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:114-123) composes selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions) FIRST via the ?? chain, and that function (allowance-rate-service.ts:33-44) sorts ACTIVE versions by updatedAt/createdAt and ignores workDate; selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion (the workDate-aware one, :19-31) is only reached when the first returns null (i.e., no active version exists). So the auditor's description of the control flow is correct.

But the auditor's CAUSAL claim — that the relegated workDate-aware selector would otherwise have priced backdated work with the rate effective on workDate — is false, which collapses the finding. Two facts from the source break the chain:

1) Single-active invariant. saveStoredAllowanceRateVersion (operations-storage-service.ts:1588-1600) runs, whenever a version is saved with status==='active', UPDATE allowance_rate_versions SET status='retired' ... WHERE id<>? AND status='active'. This retires ALL other active versions on activation (present since 0.2.1, commit adbcb21, not new in 0.4.30). The fixtures encode the same model (allowance-rate-fixtures.ts: rate-2026-1 retired, only rate-2026-2 active). listStoredAllowanceRateVersions reads this DB state (operations-storage-service.ts:1399-1414), so at most ONE version is active at runtime. With one active version, selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion can only return that one version, and there is no 'latest among several active' to mispick.

2) The fallback selector cannot reach the historically-correct rate either. selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion ALSO filters status==='active' (allowance-rate-service.ts:24) before the date-range filter. After a rate change the OLD (effective-on-workDate) version is 'retired', so it is excluded by BOTH selectors. Thus reordering them would NOT make backdated work use the old rate — the old rate is unreachable by design. The auditor's premise that the workDate selector yields the correct backdated version is therefore wrong.

Belt-and-suspenders mitigations: the active rate is snapshotted into the calculation at compute time (approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:352,365) and an existing calculation for an approval is returned without recompute (282-287), so already-approved pay is immune to later rate changes. Edit also forbids backdating effectiveFrom below today (operations-storage-service.ts:1502-1504).

Residual real issue (different and minor): a genuinely backdated NEW approval — work performed before a rate change but first approved/calculated after it — is priced with the current active rate, not the retired rate that was effective on the work date, because retired rates are never used for historical pricing. This is a data-model/policy limitation, not the selector-precedence bug claimed, and is an edge case. Net: defect AS STATED is refuted; a lesser, distinct concern remains at low severity.

criticalFindings.title: Forked duty interpretation over an unconstrained dutyCode string (no single source of truth)
criticalFindings.detail: dutyCode is `string` with no enum/brand (model.ts:119 ShiftPatternStep, :242 MonthlyScheduleItem). Restore classifies duty purely by start-time/overnight window and explicitly ignores the literal letter (monthly-schedule-restore-service.ts:278-318 classifyGridDutyCode), while the schedule-return parser matches the literal dutyCode string equality (schedule-return-performance-parser.ts:701-714). Two divergent interpretations of the same field, neither preventable by the type, is a structural correctness hazard for time/pay computation.

verification.finding: Forked duty interpretation over an unconstrained dutyCode string (no single source of truth)
verification.reasoning:
All cited lines exist verbatim: model.ts:119 (ShiftPatternStep.dutyCode: string) and :242 (MonthlyScheduleItem.dutyCode: string) are unbranded strings; monthly-schedule-restore-service.ts:281-318 classifyGridDutyCode classifies by start-time/overnight window and ignores the literal letter; schedule-return-performance-parser.ts:701-714 resolveScheduleItemByDutyCode matches item.dutyCode === dutyCode literally. BUT the framing "two divergent interpretations of the same field" is a category error. These are two cooperating stages on opposite sides of a normalization boundary, not two readers disagreeing about one value.

Trace: classifyGridDutyCode is a WRITER. In parseMonthlyScheduleItemsFromExportedPlan it builds a D/E/N-keyed dutyTimeSources map (buildDutyTimeSourceMap, restore svc 325-351) and persists each item with dutyCode set to the grid code (D/E/N), restore svc:458, paired with the time window classified into that same bucket. It deliberately ignores the pattern's own letter precisely so A/B/C 3교대 patterns normalize to the grid D/E/N space. So after restore every monthly_schedule_items.duty_code is in {D,E,N,O}.

resolveScheduleItemByDutyCode is a READER of that already-normalized field. Its dutyCode argument has type SchedulePlanWorkingDutyCode = "D"|"E"|"N" (schedule-plan.ts:10) and at every call site (parser 742/793/828/1054/1099/1179) originates from iterating layout.supportedWorkingDutyCodes (D/E/N) — never a raw pattern letter. The schedule it queries (context.schedule) comes from listStoredMonthlySchedules() (resolveScheduleContext parser:635-637), i.e. the stored D/E/N-coded rows. So literal equality matches D/E/N against D/E/N — the correct operation, not a divergent interpretation.

Crucially, the OTHER writer of the same field also normalizes to D/E/N: saveStoredMonthlySchedule (storage svc:169, INSERT duty_code at :220/:269) is called from register-workforce-handlers.ts:320 (UI monthly-schedules:save), whose items come from buildMonthlyScheduleDraft. That function sets dutyCode = normalizeStepDutyCode(step.dutyCode, dutyCodeMap) (monthly-schedule-draft.ts:399), and normalizeStepDutyCode (:172-183) returns strictly "D"|"E"|"N"|"O". So NO path persists a raw A/B/C pattern letter into the field the parser reads. There is in fact a single source of truth for the stored field's vocabulary: the export/grid D/E/N space, and both writers honor it.

The dead holiday resolver resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable (parser:725-766, always returns {foundNoneMarker:false, scheduleItem:null}) is unrelated to this claim. The only genuine residual is that dutyCode is typed as bare string rather than a branded D/E/N/O union — a real but low-severity type-hygiene weakness that does not, between these two functions, enable the claimed pay/time drift, because the runtime normalization is enforced at both write sites. Not a high-severity structural correctness hazard; downgrade to low and refute the "forked interpretation" characterization.

criticalFindings.title: Dead holiday resolver still invoked in the performance parser
criticalFindings.detail: resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable (schedule-return-performance-parser.ts:725-766) loops over reschedule cells but its inner body only `continue`s (746-758), computes nothing, and unconditionally returns {foundNoneMarker:false, scheduleItem:null}. It is still wired into the parse path at :1274, so a real holiday slot it was meant to resolve always falls through to null — contributing to the 'silently 0 minutes' class of bug.

verification.finding: Dead holiday resolver still invoked in the performance parser (resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable, schedule-return-performance-parser.ts:725-766, wired at :1274)
verification.reasoning:
The structural claim is REAL and PRESENT in 0.4.30. resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable (725-766) is dead: it loops over input.layout.rescheduleDateCells, continues on date mismatch (738-740), and its innermost loop (746-758) reads regularName/changedName but its only statement is `if (isVirtualOriginalWorker(regularName) && isNoneActualWorker(changedName)) { continue; }` (755-757) — a no-op continue at the end of the loop body that computes, accumulates, and returns nothing. There is exactly one return, unconditional, `{ foundNoneMarker: false, scheduleItem: null }` (762-765). It is still invoked at 1274 when !directScheduleItem && isVirtualOriginalWorker(originalWorker). So far the auditor is correct.

However, the severity/impact framing ('a real holiday slot it was meant to resolve always falls through to null — contributing to silently 0 minutes') is OVERSTATED. The function's null/false return is behaviorally inert because every consumer already compensates: (a) the result feeds scheduleItem = directScheduleItem ?? virtualScheduleItem?.scheduleItem ?? slotScheduleItem?.scheduleItem ?? null (1306-1310), where slotScheduleItem comes from the REAL, working resolver resolveScheduleItemFromReturnedDutySlot (1281-1291, defined at 768+); (b) the row-drop guard at 1293-1300 only `continue`s when isVirtualOriginalWorker(originalWorker) && !directScheduleItem && !virtualScheduleItem?.foundNoneMarker && !slotScheduleItem — since the dead fn always returns foundNoneMarker:false that term is constant-false, but the row is dropped only if slotScheduleItem is ALSO null, so the working slot resolver governs the actual outcome, not the dead function. Deleting resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable would change no observable behavior because virtualScheduleItem?.scheduleItem and virtualScheduleItem?.foundNoneMarker already evaluate as null/false everywhere. Therefore it is genuine dead/misleading code (wasted Excel cell reads, confusing maintenance hazard) but NOT an active cause of wrong pay or silently-dropped rows. Severity medium is not justified; low is correct. Same condition the 2026-06-13 audit described — STILL-OPEN as dead code, but its payroll impact is nil given the working slot-resolver fallback.

criticalFindings.title: Zero SQL foreign keys; referential integrity is hand-rolled in service code
criticalFindings.detail: Repo-wide grep for FOREIGN KEY across src/ returns nothing. Table relationships (employee↔site, performance↔approval↔allowance) are enforced only by imperative service logic, so an incomplete restore (finding above) or hand-moved-orphan path can leave dangling rows the DB will never reject. For a payroll dataset this removes the last automatic backstop.
criticalFindings.evidence: grep -rln 'FOREIGN KEY' src/ → no matches; src/main/services/sqlite-storage-service.ts (schema, 30KB) contains no REFERENCES

verification.finding: Zero SQL foreign keys; referential integrity is hand-rolled in service code
verification.reasoning: Traced the actual 0.4.30 schema. Repo-wide case-insensitive grep for `FOREIGN KEY` across src/ returns zero matches; grep for `REFERENCES` matches only unrelated files (PDF/Excel/chart "references", a test helper) and produces NO match inside the schema body of sqlite-storage-service.ts. The schema (migrateDatabase, lines 35-628) declares 35 CREATE TABLE statements, every one using `id TEXT PRIMARY KEY`. Numerous columns are de-facto relational links — employee_site_assignments.employee_id/site_id (l.74-75), wage_rates.employee_id (l.90), shift_patterns.site_id (l.103), performance_approvals.file_id/entry_id (l.479-480), hidden_approved_performance_rows.approval_id (l.504), allowance_calculations.performance_approval_id/rate_version_id (l.518,531), allowance_calculation_items.calculation_id (l.551), allowance_approvals.calculation_id (l.587), allowance_proposal_approvals.export_record_id (l.616) — yet none carries a REFERENCES clause or any FK. Beyond the missing declarations, there is also no `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` anywhere; the only PRAGMAs are `journal_mode = WAL` (l.37) and a WAL checkpoint elsewhere. node:sqlite, like all SQLite, leaves FK enforcement OFF by default per-connection, so even hypothetical FKs would be inert. The DB is opened plainly at l.792 `new DatabaseSync(resolvedDbPath)` then migrateDatabase — no FK pragma on open. Thus referential integrity is enforced solely by imperative service logic. The claim is factually exact and not overstated. Severity medium is correctly calibrated: this is a defense-in-depth gap, not itself a payment miscalculation. It does not corrupt money on its own, but it removes the last automatic backstop, so it directly amplifies the higher-severity restore-drops-4-tables finding and the hand-moved-orphan path (a partial/incomplete restore leaves dangling allowance/approval rows the DB will silently accept). Not high (no standalone wrong-pay mechanism), not low (for a payroll dataset the missing backstop is materially consequential). Real and STILL-PRESENT in 0.4.30.

criticalFindings.title: Quality gate exists in CI but is not on the publish path
criticalFindings.detail: .github/workflows/ci.yml (added today, 8b855ed/e45e6fd) runs typecheck + npm test + build on every push/PR — a genuine improvement. criticalFindings.title: JSON restore silently drops 4 tables of pay/approval history
criticalFindings.detail: JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER (database-migration-service.ts:74-104) and the restore loop (tableNames at :2741, forEach at :2787) re-create only a fixed 30-table list. Four tables that exist in the schema — access_logs, allowance_approvals, allowance_proposal_approvals, hidden_approved_performance_rows (all confirmed via `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`) — are NOT in the list, so on restore their rows are silently dropped. In a payroll app this is loss of approval and pay-record history with no error surfaced.

verification.finding: JSON restore silently drops 4 tables of pay/approval history (access_logs, allowance_approvals, allowance_proposal_approvals, hidden_approved_performance_rows) — database-migration-service.ts JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER omits them.
verification.reasoning:
Traced the full restore path in 0.4.30 (commit d08080f, version 0.4.30). The defect is REAL and STILL-OPEN.

Schema: sqlite-storage-service.ts defines 34 user tables via CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS. The 4 cited tables all exist: access_logs (:349), hidden_approved_performance_rows (:502), allowance_approvals (:585), allowance_proposal_approvals (:607).

Restore allowlist: database-migration-service.ts JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER (:74-104) contains exactly 29 tables. normalizeJsonBackupSnapshot adds only "app_setting_entries" (:2741), which is intentionally NOT restored (its presence merely triggers a warning at :2802-2804). The restore loop importJsonBackupIntoCurrentDatabase iterates ONLY JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER (forEach at :2787-2794) and inserts rows for those 29 tables. The 4 cited tables appear in NEITHER list, so they receive zero rows.

Why this is true DATA LOSS, not a harmless in-place skip: runDatabaseMigrationUpdate (:3063-3136) builds a FRESH empty temp DB (restore-*.sqlite, :3085-3088), initializes it so schema CREATE TABLE statements run (the 4 tables exist but empty, :3093-3097), imports JSON into it (only the 29 tables get rows, :3099), then replaceDatabaseFileAtomically OVERWRITES the live DB file with the temp file (:3108). The old live DB — which held rows in all 4 tables — is wholly discarded. So the 4 tables end up permanently empty after a restore.

Symmetry break confirms intent vs. behavior gap: the BACKUP side (database-backup-service.ts listUserTableNames :45-55) dumps EVERY user table via sqlite_master, so the JSON backup faithfully CONTAINS all 4 tables' rows. The user believes they have a complete backup; restore silently throws 4 tables away. No error or warning is surfaced for the dropped tables (only app_setting_entries gets a warning).

Load-bearing in payroll context (confirmed via readers/writers): allowance_approvals (allowance-approval-service.ts INSERT :128 / SELECT :70) and allowance_proposal_approvals (allowance-proposal-approval-service.ts INSERT :130 / SELECT :69) are the authoritative approval state for overtime-allowance payments and 품의서 proposals. hidden_approved_performance_rows (performance-approved-row-visibility-service.ts INSERT :86 / SELECT :36) controls which approved rows are excluded from view/processing. Restoring from backup (a routine DR/migration op) silently loses the entire allowance-approval and proposal-approval history and resurfaces previously-hidden rows.

Minor imprecision in the auditor's framing (does not change verdict): the list is 29 entries (not "30"); counting app_setting_entries makes 30 referenced names but it is deliberately not restored. The omission of exactly the 4 named tables is correct. All cited line numbers (:74-104, :2741, :2787, the 4 CREATE TABLE statements) are accurate. If anything the finding UNDERSTATES the mechanism: it's not an in-place insert that skips tables, it's a full atomic file replacement with a freshly-built DB, guaranteeing the old rows are gone.

Severity remains critical: silent, unrecoverable loss of approval and pay-record history in a payroll app, on the most safety-critical operation (restore-from-backup), with no error surfaced. None of the 0.4.30 additive changes (auto-archive holiday gate, hand-moved-orphan recovery, official un-archive) touch this path.

criticalFindings.detail: toRateTable (approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:114-123) tries selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions) FIRST in the `??` chain, before the workDate-aware selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion. selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion (allowance-rate-service.ts:33-44) ignores workDate entirely — it filters active versions and sorts by updatedAt/createdAt desc, returning the most-recently-edited version. verification.finding: Rate-version selection ignores workDate → backdated pay uses wrong rate (toRateTable calls selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion before the workDate-aware selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion)
verification.reasoning: Trace of the actual 0.4.30 source (HEAD on feature/perf-recovery-cleanup-A): toRateTable in approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:114-123 builds its `version` via a `??` chain whose FIRST operand is selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions). That function (allowance-rate-service.ts:33-44) takes NO workDate: it filters status==="active", sorts by updatedAt ?? createdAt desc (tiebreak effectiveFrom desc), and returns [0]. The workDate-aware selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion({targetDate}) (lines 19-31, which filters active versions whose [effectiveFrom,effectiveTo] contains the workDate) is only the SECOND operand, so it is reached only when the first returns null — i.e. only when there are zero active versions. Whenever an active version exists, the applied-version branch wins and workDate is never consulted. The chosen versionId is baked into the immutable snapshot at line 352 (allowanceRateVersionId: selectedRate.versionId) and the record at 381-382, and the version's multipliers flow into the pay via buildAllowanceRateTable(version) at line 132/365 → createAllowanceCalculationSnapshot rateTable at 365. So a wrong version = wrong multipliers = wrong overtime pay, permanently snapshotted. git blame shows the offending `selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions) ??` line was added in commit adbcb21 (0.2.1, 2026-03-31) and is unchanged through 0.4.30 → STILL-OPEN. The finding's file:line citations are all accurate. One scope correction: the DETAIL implies multiple active versions coexist and the "most-recently-edited" one wins arbitrarily. In the SQLite-backed production store that is not the steady state — saving any version as active retires all other actives (operations-storage-service.ts:1588-1599: UPDATE ... SET status='retired' WHERE id<>? AND status='active'), so there is normally exactly ONE active version. With one active version the two selectors AGREE whenever the workDate lies inside that version's effective window; they DIVERGE precisely for a BACKDATED workDate that predates the current active version's effectiveFrom (falling into a now-retired version's window). In that case selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion returns the current active version (wrong, newer multipliers) while selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion would have returned null and let the year/effectiveFrom fallbacks pick a closer historical version. So the exploit is narrower than "every approval is random" but exactly matches the stated backdated-pay scenario, and the contrasting sibling code performance-overtime-repair-service.ts:44-48 correctly puts selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion({targetDate}) FIRST, proving the calculation-service ordering is the anomaly. Severity stays critical: this is a payroll app, the error is silent, it bakes a wrong rate into an immutable pay snapshot, and the trigger (approving a backdated work date after a rate-version change) is a normal real-world event for retroactive/late approvals.

I traced both cited sites in the 0.4.30 source.

CLAIM 1 (monthly-schedule-draft.ts:182 maps an unrecognized WORKING code to 'O', "dropping a working slot") is REFUTED. normalizeStepDutyCode returns 'O' at line 178-180 only for genuine off-duty codes (OFF_DUTY_CODES = {X,OFF,O}) — correct behavior. The line-182 `dutyCodeMap.get(normalizedCode) ?? 'O'` only reaches the 'O' fallback if a NON-off code is absent from dutyCodeMap. But dutyCodeMap is built by buildExportDutyCodeMap → getWorkingDutyCodes(pattern), which collects every non-off code across getPatternCycles(pattern) (lines 137-155, 349). The step.dutyCode passed in (line 399) comes from teamCycleContext.cycle.steps, and teamCycleContextMap is built from the SAME getPatternCycles(pattern) (lines 232-265). So any working step code is guaranteed present in the map → the 'O' fallback is unreachable for working codes (dead-defensive only). Furthermore the map VALUES are always valid D/E/N: buildShiftPatternDutySlotMap assigns each working code a slot in [0,shiftCount-1] and targetCodes has exactly shiftCount entries, so targetCodes[slot] is never undefined for a working code. Finally, this function (buildMonthlyScheduleDraft) is the schedule-DRAFT generation path for the editor (ScheduleManagementScreen.tsx:1211), NOT the performance-intake/pay-derivation layer the finding claims — the auditor mislocated it.

The function is genuinely dead: its inner loops only `continue` and it unconditionally returns {foundNoneMarker:false, scheduleItem:null} (lines 762-765). A null schedule does produce totalWorkMinutes:0 via createWorkTimeFromScheduleItem (lines 863-871). HOWEVER: (a) it is only the middle link of a three-way `directScheduleItem ?? virtualScheduleItem?.scheduleItem ?? slotScheduleItem?.scheduleItem` chain on the SUBSTITUTE path (line 1306-1310), fully superseded by resolveScheduleItemFromReturnedDutySlot which builds a real item via resolveScheduleItemByDutyCode (lines 822-829); (b) the documented HOLIDAY-zero root-cause path (lines 1171-1194) does NOT use this dead resolver at all — commit 455f4a8 added the duty-code-slot fallback resolveScheduleItemByDutyCode there explicitly to avoid "collapsing to 0 minutes" (comment 1172-1176); (c) when all resolvers are null the code pushes a warning alert (lines 1330-1335) and on the substitute virtual-worker path actually `continue`s/skips the row (line 1293-1300) rather than emitting a 0-pay entry.

verification.reasoning:
I read the cited source in src/main/services/schedule-return-performance-parser.ts and traced both the function body and its single call site.

BODY (lines 725-766): The function declares a return type {foundNoneMarker:boolean; scheduleItem:MonthlyScheduleItem|null}. Its outer loop iterates layout.rescheduleDateCells and `continue`s when workDate !== input.workDate (738-740). The middle loop iterates supportedWorkingDutyCodes (742). The inner slot loop (746-758) computes regularName (747-749) and changedName (750-753) via side-effecting cell reads, but the ONLY statement using them is `if (isVirtualOriginalWorker(regularName) && isNoneActualWorker(changedName)) { continue; }` (755-757) — a no-op `continue` that merely advances the slot index. No variable is hoisted out of the loops, no accumulator is mutated, and there is no early return anywhere in the loops. Execution always falls through to the unconditional `return { foundNoneMarker: false, scheduleItem: null }` (762-765). The `schedule` field on the input type (728) is never referenced in the body. Therefore the function provably always returns the constant {foundNoneMarker:false, scheduleItem:null}, and regularName/changedName are dead computations.

CALL SITE: Grep confirms exactly two occurrences — the definition (725) and one call (1274). The call is at lines 1272-1280 (the auditor cited :1274, which is the precise line of the `resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable({` expression; the call statement spans 1272-1280). It is reachable only when `!directScheduleItem && isVirtualOriginalWorker(originalWorker)`, otherwise virtualScheduleItem is null. Downstream consumption proves the call is inert: line 1296 `!virtualScheduleItem?.foundNoneMarker` is always true (foundNoneMarker always false); line 1308 `virtualScheduleItem?.scheduleItem` in the `??` chain is always null and never contributes a schedule item; line 1319 `!virtualScheduleItem?.scheduleItem` is always true. So whether the function is invoked or replaced by a literal `null`, downstream behavior is identical apart from the throwaway cell reads.

The defect is REAL and STILL PRESENT in 0.4.30 (matches prior finding #6, status STILL-OPEN). It is not overstated: it genuinely is dead/misleading code reachable on the holiday-pay parse path. It is also not understated: the function always returns null and null is fully handled by the consuming logic, so it does NOT produce a wrong payment or silently drop pay — the holiday-table fallback simply never resolves anything (cases fall through to slotScheduleItem at 1281-1291 or are skipped at 1293-1300). criticalFindings.detail: resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable iterates reschedule date cells and duty slots but its inner loop body is a single no-op `continue` and it unconditionally returns {foundNoneMarker:false, scheduleItem:null}. verification.finding: Dead holiday/None-marker resolver permanently returns null (resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable in schedule-return-performance-parser.ts)
verification.reasoning:
Verified against current 0.4.30 source (package.json version 0.4.30; file last modified by commit 455f4a8/e6fad10).

DEFINITION (lines 725-766): resolveVirtualScheduleItemFromHolidayTable iterates input.layout.rescheduleDateCells (734), matches the workDate (738-740), then loops supportedWorkingDutyCodes (742) and regular/changed slot columns (746). The only conditional in the inner body is `if (isVirtualOriginalWorker(regularName) && isNoneActualWorker(changedName)) { continue; }` (755-757) — a pure no-op: the branch it guards does nothing, and there is no other statement in the loop body. After both loops the function unconditionally returns `{ foundNoneMarker: false, scheduleItem: null }` (762-765). So both return fields are constants regardless of input. CONFIRMED.

CALL SITE (buildSubstituteEntries, 1231-1373): virtualScheduleItem is computed at 1272-1280 only when `!directScheduleItem && isVirtualOriginalWorker(originalWorker)`, else null. Tracing the three downstream uses:
 (1) Skip gate 1293-1300: `isVirtualOriginalWorker(originalWorker) && !directScheduleItem && !virtualScheduleItem?.foundNoneMarker && !slotScheduleItem`. Because foundNoneMarker is always false, `!virtualScheduleItem?.foundNoneMarker` is always true, so this clause never blocks the skip — the row is dropped unless slotScheduleItem (the duty-slot path, 1281-1290) provides a value.
 (2) scheduleItem selection 1306-1310: `directScheduleItem ?? virtualScheduleItem?.scheduleItem ?? slotScheduleItem?.scheduleItem ?? null`. virtualScheduleItem.scheduleItem is always null, so this operand never contributes time.
 (3) Signature 1362-1363 records virtualFoundNoneMarker (always false) and the null virtualScheduleItem.
All three of the auditor's claims hold: the holiday-table recovery branch can never contribute pay time; a virtual-original-worker row either falls through to the slot path or is skipped at 1293-1300. CONFIRMED.

The prior code returned `{ foundNoneMarker: true, scheduleItem: resolveScheduleItemByDutyCode(input.schedule, dutyCode, workDate) }`; commit e6fad10 (2026-06-12, 실적관리.계산표시안정화) replaced that with `continue`. So a previously-working recovery was deliberately gutted in place rather than removed.

It is NOT a mispay vector: resolveScheduleItemByDutyCode (the function the gutted branch used to call) is still live on three other paths (lines 828 slot resolver, 1099/1179 holiday entries — the 455f4a8 fallback), and virtual/holiday rows are now routed through the slot/duty-code path (slotScheduleItem) which provides a genuine time recovery. The defect is dead/misleading logic on the substitute pay path — a maintenance and code-clarity hazard that overstates the apparent recovery coverage — not a payment-correctness defect. The auditor's 'masks an unimplemented recovery / inflates the apparent safety net' framing is fair but slightly overstated since a parallel real recovery exists. Severity unchanged at medium.

criticalFindings.title: Individually-missing schedule row yields 0 minutes with only a non-blocking WARNING
criticalFindings.detail: When a holiday or substitute worker is not found in the (possibly partially restored) monthly schedule, createWorkTimeFromScheduleItem returns all-zero minutes (parser:863-872) and the parser attaches WARNING-severity alerts ('근무표 저장 정보를 찾지 못했습니다', '개인 근무표 기준을 찾지 못해…'). The approval gate only blocks on ERROR-severity alerts (performance-approval-flow-service.ts:147-149), so a 0-minute row is not blocked by the alert check. In practice it is usually saved by the secondary gate (startTime/endTime required, approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:308-314, which errors when the schedule item is absent and times are undefined), and the new 455f4a8 duty-slot fallback (parser:1177-1187) further narrows the gap — but the policy still leans on downstream gates rather than treating a 0-payable-minute holiday/substitute row as a first-class blocking error.

verification.finding: Individually-missing schedule row yields 0 minutes with only a non-blocking WARNING (holiday/substitute path in schedule-return-performance-parser.ts), relying on a downstream calculation gate rather than a first-class blocking error.
verification.reasoning:
Traced the full path in 0.4.30 and every cited claim checks out, including the finding's own caveats.

1) Zero-minute production: createWorkTimeFromScheduleItem(null,...) returns totalWorkMinutes/base/overtime/night = 0 with startTime and endTime ABSENT (undefined) at parser:863-872. buildEntry copies workTime.startTime/endTime straight into the entry (parser:1010-1011), so a missing schedule item produces an entry with undefined start/end times.

2) Warning-only severity for the INDIVIDUALLY-missing case: when context.schedule exists but this worker/duty is not in it, only "warning"-severity alerts are attached — holiday virtual/empty-slot path 1108-1119, holiday named-worker path 1182-1193, substitute path 1312-1336 ("근무표 저장 정보를 찾지 못했습니다", "개인 근무표 기준을 찾지 못해…", "원래 근무표 정보를 찾지 못했습니다"). No error escalation occurs for these rows.

3) The whole-schedule-missing case is DIFFERENT and is hard-blocked: markMissingScheduleRows (parser:1635-1661) prepends an ERROR-severity alert ("월간 근무표 저장본이 없어 근무시간을 산출할 수 없습니다"), but it is invoked ONLY when scheduleContext.schedule is null (parser:1696-1698). Test parser.test.ts:925-933 asserts this error alert on the 0-minute holiday/substitute entries. So only the individually-missing-within-present-schedule case stays warning-only — exactly the finding's scope.

4) Approval alert gate blocks only error: validateApprovalEntry filters severity === "error" (flow-service:147-149); a warning-only 0-minute row passes this gate.

5) Secondary calc gate catches it: runApprovedAllowanceCalculationForApproval errors with ALLOWANCE_WORK_TIME_REQUIRED when startTime/endTime are missing (calc-service:308-314); the approval flow then deletes the just-created approval + calculation records and returns ok:false (flow-service:181-190). I confirmed all approval traffic routes through this single function (flow-service:179; the only other caller, calc-service:506, recalculates already-approved records). So no 0-minute holiday/substitute row can be paid or persisted as approved — the gate is load-bearing and works.

6) The 455f4a8 duty-slot fallback genuinely narrows the gap: holiday named-worker path now falls back to resolveScheduleItemByDutyCode when the individual worker is absent (parser:1177-1187), and the substitute path has analogous slot fallbacks (1281-1310). Test parser.test.ts:552-560 proves the common case now yields totalWorkMinutes 660 with a warning AND calculateTestAllowanceAmount > 0 — i.e., correct pay, not zero.

7) Manual hourly-rate override cannot bypass the calc gate: resolveApprovalEntry only injects hourlyRate and strips rate alerts (flow-service:114-118); it does not fabricate start/end times, so undefined-time rows are still blocked.

Conclusion: the defect is REAL and STILL PRESENT as described, and the finding is accurately stated — it is explicitly a defense-in-depth / policy weakness (leaning on a downstream gate), not an active mispayment. Because two independent gates prevent any 0-minute payment and the new fallback handles the common case, the practical money risk is minimal; medium overstates it slightly. I downgrade to low: a robustness/observability gap (a hard-resolvable row should ideally surface a first-class blocking ERROR at parse time rather than only a warning + a downstream calc-gate rejection), not a payroll-correctness defect.

criticalFindings.title: dutyCode remains an unconstrained string in the domain model
criticalFindings.detail: PatternStep.dutyCode and MonthlyScheduleItem.dutyCode are typed as plain string (model.ts:119, 242). The producer (restore, monthly-schedule-restore-service.ts) and consumer (parser) now both operate on the constrained SchedulePlanWorkingDutyCode union 'D'|'E'|'N' (schedule-plan.ts:10), so the prior A/B/C-vs-D/E/N fork that collapsed holiday minutes to 0 is reconciled in data. verification.finding: dutyCode remains an unconstrained string in the domain model
verification.reasoning: I read every cited file and traced producer-to-consumer. All three sub-claims hold against 0.4.30 source. (1) Type: model.ts:119 (ShiftPatternStep.dutyCode) and model.ts:242 (MonthlyScheduleItem.dutyCode) are plain `string`; the constrained union SchedulePlanWorkingDutyCode = "D"|"E"|"N" exists at schedule-plan.ts:10 but is not applied to either model field. (2) Reconciliation-by-convention: the producer (monthly-schedule-restore-service.ts) classifies each pattern step's TIME WINDOW to a grid code via classifyGridDutyCode (lines 281-318, pattern's own letter explicitly ignored per the comment at 276-280), iterates layout.supportedWorkingDutyCodes typed SchedulePlanWorkingDutyCode[] at line 429, and writes that D/E/N value into the persisted item at line 458. The consumer (schedule-return-performance-parser.ts) types the lookup as SchedulePlanWorkingDutyCode (line 694, 776), iterates supportedWorkingDutyCodes (line 1054), and matches item.dutyCode === dutyCode (lines 705, 711). So both ends agree on D/E/N at runtime — but only by convention, since the field type permits any string. (3) No enforcement: the storage layer round-trips the value verbatim — write at monthly-schedule-storage-service.ts:269 (item.dutyCode -> duty_code) and read at line 63 (dutyCode: row.duty_code) — with no validation and (consistent with the prior 'no SQL constraints' finding) no CHECK constraint on the TEXT column. Nothing at compile time or runtime would stop a future writer from persisting a raw pattern letter and silently re-introducing the A/B/C-vs-D/E/N drift that previously collapsed holiday minutes to 0. The defect is REAL and STILL PRESENT. However, it is correctly scoped as a latent type-safety / defense-in-depth gap, NOT a live payroll defect: the actual data-corrupting fork is reconciled in every current code path (the restore producer no longer emits raw pattern letters; it classifies by time), so today no path writes a non-D/E/N code into a schedule item. Severity low is accurate — neither under- nor over-stated. The auditor's PRIOR STATUS of 'partial' is reasonable but I would phrase it as confirmed: the runtime drift is fixed (the data reconciliation landed) while the type guard is still absent, which is exactly what the finding asserts.

criticalFindings.title: Backdated-pay rate selection is wrong AND untested
criticalFindings.detail: For approved allowances, the rate table is resolved by toRateTable(workDate) but the first selector called, selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions), ignores workDate entirely and returns the latest-updated active version (allowance-rate-service.ts:33-44); the workDate-aware selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion is only a `??` fallback (approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:115-119). Backdated approvals therefore get the newest rate. No test exercises multiple rate versions across dates to assert an older workDate uses the older rate; allowance-rate-service.test.ts has only 3 cases and never drives the production selection chain.
criticalFindings.evidence: approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts:114-123 (selectApplied called first, ignores workDate); allowance-rate-service.ts:33-44 (sorts by updatedAt, no date filter); allowance-rate-service.test.ts:9-33 (3 cases, no backdating against the applied-first chain)

verification.finding: Backdated-pay rate selection is wrong AND untested: toRateTable(workDate) resolves the rate via selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions) first, which ignores workDate and returns the latest-updated active version; the workDate-aware selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion is only a `??` fallback that is never reached when any active version exists.
verification.reasoning:
Traced the full production chain in src/main/services/approved-allowance-calculation-service.ts. runApprovedAllowanceCalculationForApproval (line 316) calls toRateTable(approvedEntry.workDate). Inside toRateTable (lines 114-123) the `??` chain evaluates selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion(versions) FIRST (line 115). That selector (allowance-rate-service.ts:33-44) filters to status==="active" and sorts purely by updatedAt desc (then effectiveFrom desc) and returns [0] — it never receives or consults workDate. Because `??` short-circuits on any non-null, the date-aware selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion({targetDate: workDate, versions}) on lines 116-119 is dead whenever at least one active version exists. The chosen versionId/versionLabel/rateTable then flow into the snapshot (line 352, 365) and the persisted allowance_calculations row (rate_version_id/label, lines 435-436), so the wrong rate is actually paid and recorded.

Concrete failure: with two simultaneously-active rate versions (e.g. a 2026-H1 version effectiveFrom 2026-01-01 and a 2026-H2 version effectiveFrom 2026-07-01, both active because the H1 one was not retired), a backdated approval for workDate 2026-02-15 should use H1. selectActiveAllowanceRateVersion would correctly pick H1 (it filters by isDateInRange). But selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion picks whichever has the newer updatedAt — the H2 version — so the backdated Feb entry is paid at the newer H2 rate. The renderer's OperationsRateSection.tsx:279 uses the same selectAppliedAllowanceRateVersion to display the single "currently applied" rate, confirming its semantics are "newest active, date-agnostic."

Why it is latent in tests: the shipped allowanceRateVersionFixtures (allowance-rate-fixtures.ts) have exactly ONE active version (rate-2026-2); rate-2026-1 is retired and rate-2027-1 is draft. With a single active version both selectors coincidentally return the same thing, so the bug never surfaces. The defect manifests only when >=2 versions are active at once — a plausible production state after a mid-year rate change where the old version is not explicitly retired.

Test-coverage claim verified as accurate: allowance-rate-service.test.ts (lines 9-33) has exactly 3 cases, all calling the selectors in isolation against the single-active-version fixture; none drive toRateTable, none build a multi-active-version fixture, none assert that an older workDate yields the older rate through the applied-first chain. approved-allowance-calculation-service.test.ts has 6 cases (lines 49,93,129,177,254) and a grep for rateVersionId/rate_version_id/workDate/effectiveFrom/selectApplied returned zero matches — it never asserts which rate version is selected. So the production selection chain is genuinely unexercised for backdating.

The defect is REAL and STILL PRESENT in 0.4.30 (package.json version 0.4.30; the cited lines are unchanged since the 0.4.14 commit per git log). It is correctly stated, not over- or under-stated. Severity critical is justified for a payroll app: it silently pays/records the wrong (newer) rate for backdated work whenever two rate versions are active, and there is no test guarding it. One honest caveat noted for calibration: the wrong payment is conditional on the operator leaving the prior version active rather than retiring it — so it does not fire on every backdated entry, only when overlapping active versions exist. That conditionality is a reason to keep it critical-with-a-note rather than to downgrade, given the impossibility of detecting it after the fact and the payroll blast radius.

verification.finding: Money rounding boundary coverage is too thin for a payroll primitive
verification.reasoning:
Trace: rounding.ts defines roundMoney = Math.round and roundUpWon = ceil-with-NaN-guard. Grep across **/*.ts shows roundMoney has ZERO production callers (only rounding.ts + rounding.test.ts); the single live payout primitive is roundUpWon, used in allowance-service.ts:80 (core total), database-migration-service.ts:1970, allowance-document-export-service.ts:1100. So the claim's framing that "roundMoney/roundUpWon are the payout primitives" is half-wrong — roundMoney is effectively dead, and deep boundary tests on it would test unused code.

The literal EVIDENCE facts are accurate: rounding.test.ts (1-32) has exactly 6 assertions (3 roundMoney, 3 roundUpWon) with one half-up, one below-half, one round-up, one NaN, and a grep confirms NO near-boundary (x.49/x.50/49999/50001), negative, or large-value/MAX cases in that file. calculation-fixtures.ts holds 13 cases (case-05 absent), all minute/time-window only. And exactly 17 of 137 test files reference total_allowance_amount/totalAllowanceAmount (confirmed: 103 .test.ts + 34 .test.tsx = 137; 17 matches).

BUT the headline conclusion ("breadth concentrates on time-window breakdown rather than won-amount correctness across rate/holiday/night permutations") is overstated and contradicted by source. allowance-service.test.ts (35-229) asserts exact won amounts across weekday-overtime (30000, 22500), legal-holiday with base+overtime+night permutation (135000), and weekday-substitute (120000) — precisely the rate/holiday/night permutations the claim says are absent. It also has a near-boundary rounding case (hourlyRate 10001 -> amount 251) and a fractional-rate precision/large-value invariant (hourlyRate 17457.07 -> 274949 with line-sum reconciliation across 2- and 3-line splits). allowance-rate-impact.test.ts (60-62) asserts before/after/delta 30000->40000/10000; approved-allowance-calculation-service.test.ts (87,172,246) asserts exact totals, summary-row reconciliation (total_allowance_amount == snapshot total), and rate-change deltas.

Net: there is a genuine but minor gap — the roundUpWon primitive itself lacks explicit ceil-boundary unit tests (e.g., exact integer vs x.0001, very large magnitudes, the integer-no-op path is covered but the fractional edges are sparse), and rounding.test.ts is indeed thin. However its real-world behavior is exercised indirectly and won-amount correctness IS tested across the permutations the claim alleges are missing. This is low-severity test thinness in a single small primitive file, not a medium-severity payroll-correctness risk. The defect is REAL but materially overstated; downgrade medium -> low.

summary: The application's structural security is genuinely good: Electron is hardened correctly (contextIsolation+nodeIntegration:false+sandbox on every BrowserWindow), the preload exposes only a fixed allowlist of named bridge methods with no generic ipcRenderer passthrough, sessions are held server-side in the main process (the renderer cannot forge them), and per-action IPC authorization is comprehensive and consistent — every money/approval mutation is gated by withActionPermission("performance-approval"/"allowance-approval") at reviewer role, every admin operation by withAdmin, and writes vs reads are cleanly separated; I found no unguarded mutating handler. Passwords use scrypt with per-user salt and timingSafeEqual, the password policy is strong, and the account-recovery path has a real, working brute-force lockout. However, the same care does NOT extend to the primary login: the default admin password is still hard-coded to "1234" (auth-password-policy.ts:1) and is always seeded, while the login lockout is dead code — recordStoredOperationAuthFailure always writes sign_in_locked_until = NULL and signIn never checks the lock, so the known-credential account is brute-forceable with zero throttling. Auto-update packages remain entirely unsigned (electron-builder build.win has no certificate and signAndEditExecutable:false), so update integrity rests solely on GitHub-hosted SHA512 with no publisher-key trust. The JSON backup dumps every table but restore re-inserts only a 28-table allowlist that omits access_logs, allowance_approvals, allowance_proposal_approvals and hidden_approved_performance_rows — silently destroying the audit trail and payment-authorization records on a restore. Secondary hardening gaps (no CSP, no navigation lockdown) exist but have limited blast radius given the strong process isolation. For a payroll app, the unthrottled known-password login plus the restore that wipes the audit/approval trail are the security-weighted concerns that hold this below a passing grade.
strengths: Electron process isolation is fully correct on every window: main.ts:184-189 sets contextIsolation:true, nodeIntegration:false, sandbox:true; the PDF (allowance-document-pdf-service.ts:851-855) and dashboard (dashboard-chart-export-service.ts) export windows that render HTML also keep nodeIntegration off and sandbox on.

Preload is minimal and safe: a single contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('appBridge', ...) (preload/index.ts:511) over a typed object of named methods, each bound to one specific channel; no raw ipcRenderer, no ipcRenderer.on/send, no generic invoke(channel) passthrough, so the renderer cannot reach arbitrary IPC channels.

Per-action IPC authorization is comprehensive and uniform: all approval/money mutations use withActionPermission('performance-approval'/'allowance-approval') at reviewer role (register-performance-handlers.ts:143-221, register-allowance-handlers.ts:107,172); all operations/user/rate/holiday admin actions use withAdmin (register-operations-handlers.ts, ~40 handlers); workforce writes use withActionPermission, reads use withSession. No unguarded mutating handler found.

Server-side session model: auth-service.ts holds currentSession in the main process and guards re-resolve it via getSessionWithRenewal(); ipc-auth-guard-service.ts properly checks expiry, password-change-required, and role. The renderer's token cannot be replayed to bypass authorization.

Credential hashing is correct: scrypt with 16-byte per-user salt and 64-byte key, compared with timingSafeEqual and length-guarded (auth-password-service.ts:40-87); strong password policy (uppercase/lowercase/digit/special, 8+) enforced on change.

Account recovery is well-built: scrypt-hashed recovery keys, a working 5-failure / 15-minute lockout (account-recovery-service.ts:28-29,138-162,247-261), forced password change, and a full SQLite backup before any recovery write.

No SQL injection in the value path: queries use prepared statements with ? placeholders; the few ${} interpolations are fixed clause fragments or identifiers sourced from hard-coded allowlists (JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER) or validated against sqlite_master and quoted via quoteSqlIdentifier (database-backup-service.ts:67,72).

Sound secret handling: GH_TOKEN is read from env and used only as a Bearer header (app-update-service.ts:104-115), never persisted or logged; access-log-service.ts stores no password/token/recovery material; the recovery flow logs the backup path but not the temporary password.
weaknesses: Default admin password remains '1234' and the login path has NO lockout/throttle, making the well-known account trivially brute-forceable.
Auto-update installers are unsigned (no Authenticode certificate in build config); update trust rests only on GitHub-hosted hashes.

verification.finding: Login lockout is dead code — known 'admin'/'1234' account is brute-forceable with zero throttling
verification.reasoning:
Traced every cited line against the current 0.4.30 source. The mechanical core of the finding is REAL and STILL PRESENT: (1) DEFAULT_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD = "1234" (auth-password-policy.ts:1) is unconditionally seeded for user-admin (auth-bootstrap-service.ts:46-48 maps user-admin -> "1234"; lines 214-233 always write/resolve that default unless an env override or prior retirement exists). (2) recordStoredOperationAuthFailure increments sign_in_failure_count but ALWAYS sets sign_in_locked_until = NULL (operations-storage-service.ts:2008-2016, verbatim) — there is NO code path anywhere that ever writes a non-NULL sign_in_locked_until for the password login flow (grep confirms NULL at 1980/2011/2059 only; the only working lock is the SEPARATE account_recovery_locked_until recovery-key flow in account-recovery-service.ts). (3) signIn (auth-service.ts:104-118) validates the password without ever reading sign_in_locked_until or signInFailureCount, so no number of failures ever blocks a login attempt. This is codified as intended behavior by auth-service.test.ts:220-266, which asserts that after 5 failures signInLockedUntil is undefined and the 6th attempt with the correct password still succeeds. Stale audit docs (artifacts/.../SECURITY_REVIEW.md:90, HANDOFF_CONTEXT.md:64) claim "5회 실패 시 15분 잠금" but the source proves that lockout never fires. So the "dead lockout / zero throttling / unlimited online password guessing" claim is fully accurate and applies to EVERY account.

Where the finding is OVERSTATED is the "unauthenticated takeover to all approval/payment/admin functions" impact framing for the specific admin/1234 path. The admin user is seeded with must_change_password = 1 (operations-storage-service.ts:950). signIn returns ok:true but carries passwordChangeRequired:true (auth-service.ts:127). That flag is hard-gated at BOTH layers: the renderer routes to PasswordChangeScreen and never renders DashboardShell (App.tsx:350-362), AND — critically — the main-process IPC boundary enforces it: every operational IPC goes through withSession/withActionPermission/withAdmin (main.ts:78-109), which call requireOperationalSession/requireRoleSession (main.ts:69-76), which return AUTH_PASSWORD_CHANGE_REQUIRED while the flag is set (ipc-auth-guard-service.ts:48-62) and also enforce role (lines 64-79). So an attacker who logs in with the publicly-known admin/1234 on a fresh install cannot invoke ANY approval/payment/admin IPC until the password is rotated — it is not a turnkey takeover. The genuine, still-real risk is the absence of brute-force protection on all accounts (admin after rotation, operator, reviewer), enabling unlimited unthrottled online guessing against any weak password — serious for a payroll app, but not the "publicly-knowable-1234 = instant full takeover" critical the title implies. Hence: defect confirmed as real and present, severity corrected critical -> high.

criticalFindings.detail: Backup dumps every user table via sqlite_master (database-backup-service.ts:46-55,72), so access_logs, allowance_approvals, allowance_proposal_approvals and hidden_approved_performance_rows are all written into the backup JSON. But importJsonBackupIntoCurrentDatabase only re-inserts the fixed JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER allowlist (database-migration-service.ts:74-104,2787-2794), which excludes all four. A backup→restore round-trip therefore silently destroys the entire access/audit log and the allowance/proposal approval records that authorize payment, with no warning. app_users IS now in the list (line 95), so this is narrower than before but still drops audit + approval-authorization data.

verification.finding: JSON restore omits 4 tables (access_logs, allowance_approvals, allowance_proposal_approvals, hidden_approved_performance_rows) — backup→restore round-trip silently destroys the audit trail and payment-authorization records.
verification.reasoning:
Traced the full backup→restore round-trip in CURRENT 0.4.30 source and the defect is real and worse than "narrower than before" implies — the lost data is permanently destroyed, not merely left behind.

BACKUP side (database-backup-service.ts): listUserTableNames() (lines 38-56) enumerates EVERY user table via sqlite_master with no allowlist; listBackupTableSnapshots() (58-82) reads every row of each; buildJsonBackupSnapshot() (84-101) writes them all into tables keyed by name. So the JSON backup DOES contain all four tables' rows (they exist as real tables — confirmed CREATE TABLE in sqlite-storage-service.ts:349 access_logs, :502 hidden_approved_performance_rows, :585 allowance_approvals, :607 allowance_proposal_approvals).

RESTORE side (database-migration-service.ts): JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER (74-104) lists 29 tables; none of the four appear (app_users IS now present at line 95, so app_users is no longer dropped — that part of the prior finding is fixed). normalizeJsonBackupSnapshot() (2727-2754) only parses tables in JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER + app_setting_entries, so the four tables are not even read from the JSON. importJsonBackupIntoCurrentDatabase() (2773-2800) iterates only JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER and INSERTs rows.

CRITICAL — it is a file REPLACE, not additive: runDatabaseMigrationUpdate() (3063-3124) builds a fresh empty temp DB (3085-3097), imports only the allowlisted tables into it (3099-3105) — leaving the four tables schema-created but EMPTY — then at line 3108 calls replaceDatabaseFileAtomically(currentSettings.databasePath, tempDatabasePath). In database-replacement-service.ts that function renames the live DB to a .migration-backup-<ts> file (line 38), renames the temp DB over the live path (42), then DELETES the renamed original (rmSync backupPath force:true, lines 43-44). So on success the original DB is permanently gone and the new live DB has zero rows in all four tables. The audit trail (access_logs) and the payment-authorization records (allowance_approvals per-row decisions; allowance_proposal_approvals = 품의 approvals with work_month/total_allowance_amount/approved_by) are destroyed.

NO WARNING confirmed: previewDatabaseMigrationUpdate() reports previewState via collectDatabaseMigrationState() (849-868), which counts only sites/employees/wages/patterns/performance/calculations — none of the four tables — so the preview cannot surface the loss either.

Severity: I keep it HIGH rather than upgrading to critical. It is destructive and silent and hits payment-authorization + audit data, which is the worst data class in a payroll app. But it requires a deliberate manual JSON restore/migration operation (not an automatic or routine path), the core money-math and the primary performance_approvals/allowance_calculations chains ARE restored, and lost rows are authorization/audit records rather than the live pay amounts themselves (recomputable payable entries survive). That places it solidly at high, not critical.

criticalFindings.title: Auto-update packages are unsigned; update integrity has no publisher-key trust
criticalFindings.detail: package.json build.win has no certificateFile/certificateSubjectName and sets signAndEditExecutable:false; there is no signing block anywhere. electron-updater (app-update-service.ts) verifies only the SHA512/blockmap from GitHub-hosted latest.yml. With no Authenticode signature, Windows SmartScreen warns on every install, and anyone able to publish to the GitHub releases repo (or who obtains GH_TOKEN) can push a malicious update that passes hash checks and installs via quitAndInstall (app-update-service.ts:478). Releases are publish.releaseType:'draft', which mitigates accidental auto-promotion but not the missing-signature trust gap.

verification.finding: Auto-update packages are unsigned; update integrity has no publisher-key trust
verification.reasoning:
I verified every load-bearing claim against the actual 0.4.30 source and the shipped artifact.

1) NO SIGNING CONFIG (confirmed). package.json build.win (lines 143-150) has only icon/target/artifactName plus `"signAndEditExecutable": false` (line 149). There is no certificateFile, certificateSubjectName, certificatePassword, signtool, or signingHashAlgorithms anywhere in package.json or any config file. A repo-wide grep (excluding node_modules) for certificateFile|certificateSubjectName|certificatePassword|CSC_LINK|CSC_KEY_PASSWORD|verifyUpdateCodeSignature|publisherName|signtool|signingHashAlgorithms returned ZERO hits in source/config — only historical release-signoff *.md logs (v0.4.0/v0.4.1) and unrelated doc "sign-off" strings. There is no separate electron-builder.{yml,yaml,json,js,toml,ts} file (Glob found none), so package.json build field is the whole config (builder-debug.yml confirms "loaded configuration file=package.json").

2) SHIPPED 0.4.30 INSTALLER IS UNSIGNED (confirmed, strongest evidence). Get-AuthenticodeSignature on release/ShiftMgmt-Setup-0.4.30-x64.exe returns Status: NotSigned ("the file is not digitally signed"), SignerCertificate empty. So the current production artifact has no Authenticode signature at all — not even self-signed. This means Windows SmartScreen/UAC shows an unknown-publisher warning, and electron-updater's optional Windows code-signature publisher check (verifyUpdateCodeSignature) has nothing to validate against. Note: the historical v0.4.1 signoff log line "signing with signtool.exe" reflects electron-builder's automatic throwaway/self-sign attempt when no cert is configured, which confers no publisher trust; regardless, the actually-shipped 0.4.30 binary is NotSigned.

3) INTEGRITY IS HASH-ONLY (confirmed). release/latest.yml (the auto-update feed) carries only sha512 + size + blockmap for ShiftMgmt-Setup-0.4.30-x64.exe — no signature/publisher field. electron-updater (app-update-service.ts) downloads via updater.downloadUpdate() (line 438) and installs via updater.quitAndInstall(false, true) at line 478 (the auditor cited 462-481, which is installDownloadedUpdate spanning those lines — accurate). The only gate before install is the SHA512/blockmap match against latest.yml, which is hosted in the same GitHub release as the binary. An attacker who can publish to the release repo controls BOTH the .exe and its latest.yml hash, so the hash check provides no trust against a malicious publisher — exactly the gap the finding describes.

4) DRAFT MITIGATION (confirmed, correctly characterized as partial). package.json publish block sets releaseType:"draft" (line 93); app-update.yml in the packaged build echoes releaseType: draft. electron-updater ignores draft releases for auto-detection, so an accidental/early draft will not auto-promote to clients. BUT scripts/publish-release-assets.mjs requires GH_TOKEN (lines 99-102) and flips the release to draft:false (line 164) to publish — so promotion to a live update is one token-gated step. The finding states this exact nuance ("mitigates accidental auto-promotion but not the missing-signature trust gap").

Severity assessment: HIGH is appropriate, not critical and not lower. It is NOT critical because exploitation requires the adversary to already hold write access to the GitHub release repo or a valid GH_TOKEN — a meaningful precondition, not a remote-unauthenticated path; and the draft+manual-promote flow plus SHA512 integrity prevent random in-flight tampering of a GitHub-hosted asset over HTTPS. It is NOT low/medium because this is a payroll app that auto-checks for updates on startup (scheduleStartupUpdateCheck) and installs with quitAndInstall; absent Authenticode publisher trust, a compromised token or repo yields silent code execution on every operator machine that runs payroll, and every legitimate install already trains users to click through SmartScreen "unknown publisher" warnings (habituating them to accept unsigned binaries). The defect is REAL and STILL PRESENT in 0.4.30, unchanged since the initial release-prep commit (1b711e2 introduced signAndEditExecutable:false). Today's 0.4.30 additive changes did not touch signing. PRIOR STATUS still-open is correct → STILL-OPEN.

verification.finding: No Content-Security-Policy and no navigation lockdown in the Electron shell

summary: The single most dangerous defect for a payroll app is unfixed in 0.4.30: the JSON backup/restore is asymmetric. The backup dumps every table via sqlite_master (database-backup-service.ts:38-56), but restore re-populates only a hardcoded 28-table whitelist (JSON_IMPORT_TABLE_ORDER, database-migration-service.ts:74-104, last touched 2026-03-24 — untouched since the prior audit). The four tables that are dropped — allowance_approvals, allowance_proposal_approvals, hidden_approved_performance_rows, access_logs — are exactly the prior-audit-1 set, all have live production writers, and allowance_proposal_approvals holds the actual 품의 payment-authorization record (work_month, total_allowance_amount, approved_by). Because restore atomically replaces and then deletes the prior live DB (database-replacement-service.ts:44), this loss is silent and irreversible, and no test catches it. Foreign keys remain entirely absent (prior-9 STILL-OPEN) and PRAGMA foreign_keys is never enabled. On the positive side, the is_effective single-copy invariant has a genuinely atomic archive+effective transaction with clear crash-recovery reasoning, and the return-to-pending flow is now transactional. But the forward approval path (approve→calculate→archive) is a compensation saga, not a true transaction, and the single-effective-copy invariant has no DB-level constraint backing it. For a payroll app where dropping approval history is the worst-case failure, the unresolved restore data-loss bug caps this dimension low.
strengths: markStoredPerformanceFileArchivedAsEffective wraps the file-archive and is_effective re-flag in a single BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK transaction (performance-file-storage-service.ts:817-853) with an explicit comment explaining the crash-safety rationale, so an interrupted approval cannot leave a (site,month) with no effective copy

The return-to-pending flow (performance-approval-flow-service.ts:653-680) now runs the row demotion plus approval/allowance cleanup in one transaction with documented reasoning that a pre-COMMIT crash yields a recoverable orphan rather than a re-approval deadlock

is_effective single-copy-per-schedule is consistently expressed as UPDATE ... SET is_effective = CASE WHEN id = ? THEN 1 ELSE 0 END WHERE schedule_key = ? (lines 806, 843), which is correct when those code paths run

The migration itself is staged safely: restore builds into a temp DB and replaceDatabaseFileAtomically renames it over the live DB, restoring the prior DB if the rename fails (database-replacement-service.ts:42-48), plus recoverOrphanedMigrationBackup handles an interrupted swap

criticalFindings.detail: The entire src tree contains zero FOREIGN KEY / REFERENCES declarations and never executes PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (only PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL at sqlite-storage-service.ts:37). (1) Grep for FOREIGN KEY|REFERENCES|foreign_keys across src returned ZERO SQL constraint declarations — every match is an unrelated identifier (e.g. listStoredPerformanceFileReferences) or a comment about ExcelJS "merge references". (2) Read the entire migrateDatabase() schema in sqlite-storage-service.ts (lines 35-628), which defines ~30 tables. Every cross-table relationship is a plain `TEXT NOT NULL` column with no constraint: performance_approvals.file_id/entry_id (lines 479-480), allowance_calculations.performance_approval_id/performance_entry_id (518-519), allowance_calculation_items.calculation_id (551), allowance_approvals.calculation_id (587), allowance_proposal_approvals.calculation_ids_json (610), allowance_document_exports.calculation_ids_json (566), hidden_approved_performance_rows.approval_id/file_id/entry_id (504-507). The acute integrity defect that actually drops pay/approval history is the separate restore-omits-4-tables finding (prior #1); FK absence compounds that class of risk but is secondary to it. high (self-rated) is appropriate — credible, not exaggerated; I do not downgrade because for a payroll system an unenforceable relational model is a material structural weakness.

criticalFindings.title: Forward approval write is a compensation saga, not an atomic transaction
criticalFindings.detail: approvePerformanceEntry -> createApprovedPerformanceRecord inserts the approval record (createPerformanceApprovalRecord, line 170) and then runs the allowance calculation separately (line 179), undoing via manual deletes on failure (lines 182-183). The outer flow then archives the file and marks it effective (lines 395-447) with more manual compensating deletes (lines 434-439). Only markStoredPerformanceFileArchivedAsEffective is internally transactional; the multi-row approve+calculate+archive sequence is not wrapped in one BEGIN/COMMIT, so a crash mid-sequence leaves a half-committed state that depends entirely on startup recovery rather than DB rollback.

criticalFindings.title: is_effective single-copy-per-schedule invariant has no DB-level constraint
criticalFindings.detail: The single-effective-copy invariant is enforced only procedurally (CASE WHEN id=? THEN 1 ELSE 0 END WHERE schedule_key=?, lines 806/843). There is no partial unique index (e.g. UNIQUE(schedule_key) WHERE is_effective=1), and the performance_files upsert (lines 381-431) writes is_effective directly from caller-supplied data. A concurrent or buggy writer can create two is_effective=1 rows for one schedule_key, which would surface duplicate effective copies of a month's approved performance with no DB guard.

verification.finding: is_effective single-copy-per-schedule invariant has no DB-level constraint (no partial/unique index); enforced only procedurally, and the performance_files upsert writes is_effective from caller-supplied data.
verification.reasoning:
Trace: The factual core of the finding is CONFIRMED. The performance_files schema (sqlite-storage-service.ts:408-433) declares only `id TEXT PRIMARY KEY`. The only indexes on the table are non-unique: idx_performance_files_status (line 435, on status/received_at) and idx_performance_files_schedule_key (lines 759-760, on schedule_key/received_at). There is NO UNIQUE constraint or partial unique index of the form UNIQUE(schedule_key) WHERE is_effective=1 anywhere. The single-effective invariant is indeed enforced purely procedurally via `is_effective = CASE WHEN id=? THEN 1 ELSE 0 END WHERE schedule_key=?` at performance-file-storage-service.ts:806 (setStoredEffectivePerformanceFile) and :843 (markStoredPerformanceFileArchivedAsEffective). The upsert (lines 381-457) does bind is_effective from detail.isEffective (line 452 -> column at 402/427), so it is caller-supplied. All cited line references check out.

HOWEVER the severity (medium) is overstated for two concrete reasons. (1) No production code path actually feeds a second is_effective=1 row through the upsert: a repo-wide search for `isEffective: true`/`isEffective = true` returns ZERO matches, so every upsert call writes is_effective=0; the bit is flipped to 1 only by the controlled CASE-WHEN function markStoredPerformanceFileArchivedAsEffective (the production approval path, performance-approval-flow-service.ts:426/539, allowance-approval-service.ts:297) which clears all siblings in the same statement, and by the migration reconstruction path (database-migration-service.ts:2392) which groups one approved file per schedule_key and dedups (line 2620-2622). Note setStoredEffectivePerformanceFile (line 794), the non-atomic variant, has NO production caller at all. (2) The "concurrent writer" threat model does not apply: the app uses node:sqlite DatabaseSync (synchronous) inside the single Electron main process, so all app writes are serialized; there is no second concurrent app writer. The only other openers of the DB file are offline operator maintenance scripts (reset-database.mjs, reset-admin-password.mjs, issue-account-recovery-key.mjs) run while the app is closed.

So this is a real defense-in-depth / hardening gap (a future buggy refactor could violate the invariant with no DB backstop), not an active data-integrity defect that currently produces duplicate effective copies or wrong pay. It is also consistent with the project-wide pattern of "no FOREIGN KEYs, enforce relations in code" (UNIQUE is only ever used on single-column natural keys: lines 41,56,327,504,541). node:sqlite/SQLite does support partial indexes, so the suggested fix is feasible. Net: REAL but LOW severity, not medium.
